summary:
Cuba's legal framework for trans people rests on the 2019 Constitution, whose Article 42 names sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories, the first constitution to do so. The 2022 Family Code, approved by referendum on 25 September 2022 with 66.87% support, legalised same-sex marriage and adoption and permits legal gender change without surgery. Consensual same-sex relations were removed from the Penal Code in 1979.

Legal gender recognition is administrative rather than surgical or judicial. The July 2025 civil-registry reform removed the remaining bureaucratic hurdles to name changes, and the Family Code already established that surgery is not a precondition.

Employment protection is narrower than the constitutional text. The Labor Code (Law 116) bars discrimination on grounds that include sexual orientation, but its article 2(b) covers orientation and does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground. A 2013 parliamentary amendment banning employment discrimination on sexual orientation passed after intense debate; Mariela Castro's proposal to extend the ban to gender identity, disability and HIV status drew support from some Christian and intellectual legislators, but only the sexual-orientation ban is confirmed as enacted.

Healthcare access has an explicit official basis. Resolution 126 (2008) brought trans healthcare into the public system, and CENESEX, the state sex-education centre, runs an official trans-care programme alongside a trans-rights campaign, working with the police and the supreme court on sexual-diversity education. In practice the economic crisis has degraded healthcare and hormone availability is reported as unreliable.

The equality settlement is contested rather than state-enforced. Opponents of the Family Code cited religious objections and feared that child-welfare provisions could be used against dissidents, while some government opponents planned to vote No purely to deny the Díaz-Canel administration a win amid the post-July-2021 crackdown, which produced more than 1,400 arrestees, and record emigration. The 25 September 2022 vote was only the fourth national election since 1959.

The counterweights are systemic rather than trans-specific. Cuba is a one-party state with no independent civil society, arbitrary-detention powers are broad, and police discretion is wide. There is no documented pattern of police targeting people for gender expression; the documented state hostility runs toward emigration and asylum claims rather than toward gender presentation.
tangentialFactors:
The historical baseline is severe and well documented. Between 1965 and 1968 the UMAP forced-labour camps held gay men, who cut cane in Camagüey roughly 60 hours a week for seven pesos a day and were subjected to electric-shock and injection experiments presented as cures. Consensual same-sex acts left the Penal Code in 1979, and Fidel Castro publicly accepted blame for the UMAP era in 2010.

Official institutions have campaigned for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s, with CENESEX running trans-rights work and engaging the police and the supreme court, a baseline that predates the 2019 Constitution.

Cuba's hostility toward departure is documented and distinct from its stance on gender expression. In January 2018 Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to eight years in prison for treason against the homeland after filing asylum claims in the Netherlands, a woman deported from the Netherlands was detained on 19 May 2018, and LGBTI activists including Nelson Gandulla of the Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation remained under monitoring. A trans visitor who sought asylum or fled could meet this machinery; a visitor who does not is unlikely to encounter it.

Compared with neighbouring jurisdictions, Cuba's constitutional and family-law settlement is among the most transformed in Latin America, though the employment-law gap on gender identity places it behind the standard its own constitution sets.
localsOnly:
Cuban workers are covered by Labor Code Law 116, which bars discrimination including on sexual orientation, but gender identity is not listed as a separate protected ground and article 2(b) addresses orientation only. Residents seeking redress therefore have a weaker statutory hook for identity-based workplace claims than for orientation-based ones.

Residents access trans healthcare through the public system under Resolution 126 (2008) and through CENESEX's official programme, which also conducts sexual-diversity education and works with police and courts. Supply-side reliability is constrained by the economic crisis.

The Family Code governs resident families directly, covering marriage, adoption, shared parental rights and codified domestic-violence penalties, and the July 2025 civil-registry reform governs name changes for people registered in Cuban civil records.

Citizens face the treason provisions if they leave to seek asylum, and independent LGBTI activists have been monitored. The absence of independent civil society means there is no organisation outside the state to which a resident can appeal.
